data.title: Xi-Trump summit signals a shifting order India must learn to navigate
data.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and United States President Donald Trump held an unprecedented trilateral summit on November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. The summit released a Trilateral Peace Declaration with four points of agreement whose implications are serious and should invite greater attention. 
That a summit among the three leaders took place at all was remarkable, and to treat it as a mere photo-op misses its significance. Its outcome should be assessed together with the outcomes of the earlier bilateral meeting between Xi Jinping and Mr Trump and between Mr Putin and Mr Trump in advance of their trilateral summit. The more important bilateral meeting was undoubtedly between Mr Xi and Mr Trump, the readout of which has some important elements: 
One, there is a reiteration of “constructive strategic stability” as a shared objective, but now there is a reference to the two sides formulating a “constructive strategic stability action plan”. This goes beyond mere rhetoric. How such an action plan will be negotiated and what its content would be remain to be seen but should be watched closely. 
Two, the language on Taiwan suggests that China believes that US policy is moving in the right direction. 
“On the Taiwan issue, the US must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-US relationship.” 
This implies that China is encouraged by the trend in US approach to Taiwan and is now more confident of achieving the goal of reunification. By the same token, this is bad news for the East and Southeast Asian partners of the US because a Taiwan unified with China will change the geopolitical landscape of the Indo-Pacific region. Japan and South Korea will be the most affected. The voices pressing for going nuclear are rising in both countries in response. 
China is comfortable with Mr  Trump and sees opportunities to advance its influence and role particularly in Asia, while the latter is still President. The Chinese readout says that Xi Jinping considers that “the guiding role of the diplomacy between the US and Chinese heads of state is irreplaceable.” 
Xi Jinping is reported to have said that “the US is very powerful; China is also very powerful” and that the two countries should “jointly lead and promote world peace and stability.”  
It is the US-China bilateral that set the stage for the trilateral, but Russia is not regarded by either as being in the same league. The feared condominium, if it emerges, will be bipolar, not tripolar. The photo-op was important for Russia, to be seen as a great power, though it is not. 
Let us analyse the Trilateral Peace Declaration whose four points were: 
One, reform of the United Nations, although it was not clear what they intended in this respect. The three signatories are referred to as “permanent members” of the Security Council, but they completely ignore the two other permanent members — France and the United Kingdom. The US allies no longer count. 
Two, the three countries plan to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. This means the end of energy sanctions against Russia. India will breathe a sigh of relief and will continue purchasing Russian oil. 
Three, the International Criminal Court (ICC) is condemned for overstepping its jurisdiction and violating “the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials”. This was an easy point of agreement as none of the three countries is a member of the ICC. Mr Putin smiled broadly when this was mentioned by Mr Trump. He has been indicted by the ICC for criminal behaviour in the assault against Ukraine. 
Four, reaffirmation of an earlier declaration of the five permanent members, all nuclear weapon states, that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”. This is reassuring specially in the wake of Russia threatening the use of nuclear weapons in the Ukraine War. There is also a commitment that the three countries would “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons”. 
This falls short of the US proposal for nuclear arms control talks among the three nuclear weapon states with the largest arsenals, which China has so far refused to join. But talks on nuclear risk reduction could be a useful starting point.
The reference to cooperation on non-proliferation is interesting. This could be a veiled reference to the Iran nuclear issue as well as the North Korea nuclear issue. For China, it could well be alluding to the threat of Japan and South Korea going nuclear, which would pose a greater challenge to China but may not be welcome to the US either.  
We should remember that even during the height of the Cold War, both the US and the then Soviet Union found common cause in preventing other countries from developing nuclear weapons. The discriminatory Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) was the result. As a nuclear weapon state that has rejected the NPT, India should watch how this element of cooperation develops among the three countries and whether there may be constraints put on countries like India.  
Could there be revival of calls for the universalisation of the NPT? China has opposed India’s membership of the Nuclear Suppliers’ Group and was virtually the last country to join the consensus in the NSG on the waiver provided to India in 2008 from the norms of the group prohibiting nuclear cooperation with countries non-signatories to the NPT. Could China try to reverse the waiver or seek it for Pakistan? How would the US react in the changed geopolitical circumstances? Could Mr Trump oblige his favourite field marshal from Pakistan? 
A great deal can happen in the two years left of Mr Trump’s tenure, and the Chinese and the Russians are determined to make the most of the opportunities this offers to them. When facts on the ground change, it is difficult to reverse course even if a new political dispensation takes charge in Washington in 2029. 
The next Xi-Trump summit is slated for mid-December this year when the G-20 summit is hosted by the US in Miami. There could even be another trilateral summit. China is gaining in influence, Russia is masking its decline, and the US is ceding space that would be difficult to retrieve. This is the challenging terrain that India must learn to navigate as we head into the new year. 
The writer is a former foreign secretary

data.title: Facing a gold loan auction? Know the steps to take before & after the sale
data.description:
The value of gold loan auctions at Manappuram Finance rose fourfold, from ₹25 crore in the June quarter to ₹100 crore in the September quarter of 2026. At ₹1,25,793 per 10 grams, gold is down 28 per cent from its January 29, 2026, high. Executives at Manappuram Finance and IIFL Finance have warned that a further decline could lead to more auctions. In such an environment, every borrower who has pledged their gold should know how auctions work. 
What triggers an auction 
Falling gold prices reduce the value of pledged jewellery and raise the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio. “If the borrower is unable to cover the margin deficit by making a partial payment to bring the LTV below the threshold within the allowed period, the lender can conduct an auction,” says Priyank Kothari, executive director, Finkurve Financial Services. 
 
An auction also follows if the loan becomes a non-performing asset (NPA). 
What to check in the notice 
Lenders send a margin-cum-auction notice for a shortfall and a loan recall-cum-auction notice for an NPA. They use registered post or speed post and also send a short message service (SMS) alert. Lenders  allow borrowers a 10- to 14-day window to clear dues or cover the shortfall. 
When you receive a notice, check the account number, itemised dues, auction date and the basis for valuation. Ask for a current statement of payments and dues. “Contact the lender and ask for a written statement of dues showing principal, interest, charges and the last date to settle,” says Adhil Shetty, chief executive officer, BankBazaar. Verify charges against the 
loan agreement and key facts statement (KFS). Pay within the 10- to 14-day window if you can. 
How to avert an auction 
Make a part-payment or pledge more gold before the auction process starts. Once this process starts, seek a settlement. Avoid verbal deals and do not sign papers that you do not fully understand. “Get a written settlement quote to halt the sale,” says Parijat Garg, a digital lending consultant. Pay thro­ugh traceable channels and coll­ect the receipt. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rules do not specifically provide for the release of a specific (favourite) piece of jewellery before an auction. But many lenders allow it if you pay the proportionate principal and in­terest. “The lender may revalue the remaining gold at current prices and seek a part-payment before releasing a specific piece,” says Shetty. 
Verify valuation, reserve price 
Lenders use purity, net weight and prevailing gold prices to value the jewellery. They exclude stones, gems and making charges. Ask for the valuation certificate and check how the lender calculated the value. “If you believe that the jewellery has been undervalued, raise a written complaint and seek reassessment before the auction,” says Prathamesh Kadival, research analyst, Bonanza. 
The RBI sets the minimum reserve price at 90 per cent of the jewellery’s current assessed value. “This can be reduced to 85 per cent after two failed auctions,” says Kothari. Keep a close eye on the reserve price, especially if gold prices are volatile. If an auction becomes inevitable, submit your bank details in writing so the lender can refund any surplus. 
What to check at the auction 
Attend the auction to check that the bidding is fair. Make sure at least three verified buyers take part and that the lender accepts only bids at or above the reserve price. “You can redeem the gold until the hammer falls,” says Garg. Borrowers and family mem­bers can generally bid. “Often, clearing the dues before the auction costs less than winning the gold back through a bid,” says Kadival. 
Claim surplus 
The lender must tell the borrower or legal heir in writing how much the sale raised and how it applied the proceeds to the dues. “If the sale recovered more than was due, claim your surplus refund within seven working days,” says Garg. 
Finally, keep your address, mobile number and email addr­ess up to date with the lender. “Notices sent to your registered address remain valid even if the contact details have not been updated,” says Kothari. Complain to the RBI Ombudsman if the lender breaches auction rules. 
Where and how gold auctions are held 
  • Auction notice must be given in at least one regional-language and one national daily
  • First auction is held in person in the lending branch’s district
  • If unsuccessful, subsequent auctions are held in adjoining districts or online
  • Cross-branch jewellery pooling can be done, subject to lender policy and regulatory requirements

data.title: Global fashion brands shift orders from Bangladesh to India amid unrest
data.description:
Global fashion retailers, including Zara and H&M, shifted nearly a tenth of their monthly orders from Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, as labour unrest disrupted production and rising costs eroded the country’s competitive edge, three factory owners said.
 
Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said, a shift that represents a major blow to a key pillar of Bangladesh’s economy and could extend beyond the current unrest.
 
Industry leaders have said rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have weakened the low-cost advantage that helped make Bangladesh the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, prompting global brands to diversify sourcing.
 
 
The protests have caused more than $400 million in production losses, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), in an industry that accounts for more than 80 per cent of Bangladesh’s export earnings and nearly 40 per cent of its manufacturing jobs.
 
Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia also benefit
 
India has emerged as the biggest beneficiary, while buyers are also looking to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to reduce supply-chain risks and improve delivery reliability, industry leaders said.
 
Those pressures intensified on Wednesday when Bangladesh approved a 36 per cent increase in the minimum wage for garment workers, the smallest rise in four decades.
 
The increase fell well short of workers’ demands to more than double wages, triggering fresh clashes with police even as Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, said the wage increase was “satisfactory” and that he hoped all workers would resume work from Saturday.
 
Industry leaders said the increase would nevertheless narrow Bangladesh’s labour-cost advantage over India, although union groups argue the wages remain low by global industry standards.
 
Babul Akhter, a union leader and workers’ representative on the government-appointed wage board, said brands should not use the unrest to justify shifting orders out of Bangladesh.
 
He said retailers already factor political instability and labour unrest into sourcing decisions, making such moves “hard to justify” and raising “serious doubts” about whether the unrest was more than an excuse.
 
Factory owners, speaking on condition of anonymity because of concerns about their relationships with international buyers, said the unrest had prompted Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer, Celio and other global brands to divert orders, with India receiving the bulk of the business.
 
Zara owner Inditex declined to comment on Reuters’ questions, while M&S, H&M and Celio did not respond to requests for comment.
 
Indian textile shares rallied after the Reuters report, with Gokaldas Exports jumping as much as 11 per cent and Trident gaining about 5 per cent. Other potential beneficiaries, including Welspun Living, KPR Mill and Vardhman Textiles, rose around 2 per cent each.
 
M Mohiuddin Chowdhury, a director of the BGMEA, said higher wages, utility and raw material costs were adding to pressure on manufacturers “at a time when buyers are demanding lower prices and competition from rival sourcing countries is intensifying”.
 
More business at risk
 
Factory owners said the bigger concern was that diversions of business could become permanent.
 
Persistent energy shortages, exacerbated by the Middle East crisis, have added to production disruptions and forced some factories to rely on more expensive alternative power sources.
 
But Chowdhury said that price became secondary when brands were under pressure to meet strict delivery deadlines.
 
India can offer buyers a delivery advantage of about a week, while Vietnam and Cambodia can cut lead times by as much as 15 days, Chowdhury said.
 
Rival sourcing hubs can typically complete production and delivery within 60 to 90 days, compared with about 120 days in Bangladesh, he added.
 
The disruptions have also created production backlogs, with manufacturers around Dhaka losing an estimated 20 to 25 production days. Some are considering overtime and costly air freight to meet delivery commitments.
 
Khan Monirul Alam, managing director of Alps Apparels Group, which mainly supplies European brands, said the unrest was already hitting new business.
 
“Since November 1, most of my buyers have stopped placing orders because of the unrest,” Alam said. “They are telling us our orders have been shifted, postponed or cancelled and that they have already found alternative solutions.”
 
Political tensions surrounding former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s possible return to Dhaka from India have added to concerns about further disruption.
 
Industry leaders said restoring stability and uninterrupted production would be critical to retaining international buyers. Chowdhury warned that orders shifted elsewhere during periods of instability might not return even after conditions improved.
 
“The challenge is restoring buyers’ confidence before temporary shifts become long-term sourcing decisions,” he said. “Brands have options. They will not wait for us if instability persists.”

data.title: Tata Sons listing, restructuring, EGM on November 30 board meet plan
data.description:
With no court injunction, the Tata Sons board meeting on November 30 is expected to discuss the issue of stock exchange listing of the holding company of the group. Restructuring of Tata Sons to keep it private, as mooted by Tata Trusts Chairman and Nominee Director Noel Tata, would also come up for deliberation. A resolution after the discussion is a likely scenario, according to sources. In the case of disagreement on the subject, voting by board members, including a casting vote by Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran is a possibility, it is learnt.
 
However, the final court verdict would determine the future course of direction for any resolution passed at the Tata Sons board meeting on November 30. The next court hearing is on January 21, 2027.    
 
In the board meeting on September 17, the two nominee directors on the Tata Sons board — Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan — had voted against and in favour of Chandrasekaran’s third term as chairman, respectively, prompting a casting vote by Independent Director Harish Manwani, who was the acting chairman for that segment of the meeting.
 
At the board meeting of November 30, Chandrasekaran’s third term is unlikely to be discussed, as a resolution on it was already passed on September 17. While the way forward on Tata Sons listing would be the main agenda on Monday, it would come up at a shareholders’ meeting soon.
 
The proposal to get an approval for an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) is listed in the meeting agenda as well. The EGM, whenever it is scheduled, would take up both the listing of Tata Sons and Chandrasekaran’s third term.
 
Tata Sons’ annual general meeting scheduled for August could not take place because of lack of quorum. A representative proposed jointly by the Sir Dorbaji Tata Trust and Sir Ratan Tata Trust must mandatorily attend a shareholders’ meeting. Since the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner froze the decision-making powers of SRTT earlier this year, a joint representative could not be appointed for an AGM.
 
Subsequently, the Registrar of Companies (RoC) allowed Tata Sons to hold the meeting by December 31, 2026. Even for an EGM, quorum will be required and, therefore, a decision by the Charity Commissioner is expected soon on the key shareholding trusts.

data.title: The boy who died in Harry Potter gets a licence to survive (and kill)
data.description:
“Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.” With this message on social media, the British Royal Family has welcomed actor Robert Pattinson after he was announced as the next James Bond. In reality, however, Pattinson has been welcomed into the domain of immortality through the character of an iconic spy.
 
Pattinson has a strange on-screen relationship with death. As a wizard, he died young. In his first big-screen appearance in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, the young actor had played an ideal Hogwarts student. However, Cedric died by the Killing Curse cast by Peter Pettigrew — or Wormtail — based on Lord Voldemort’s orders. His death was indeed an introduction to a harsh, unforgiving reality in the magical world of Harry Potter.
 
Then came Twilight, the 2008 American romantic fantasy film directed by Catherine Hardwicke. Within a few years of Cedric’s death, Pattinson played Edward Cullen — a young, handsome, wealthy vampire. Well, all vampires are immortal. Thus, as Edward Cullen in Twilight, Pattinson conquered death and possessed eternal youth. The audience was captivated by a combination of teenage romance, jealousy, attraction, and supernatural elements. And, not to forget that, despite being a vampire, Edward could easily be an ideal lover!
 
Subsequently, in his acting career, Pattinson must have wanted to come out of that image. He chose to portray unsettling, complex, and, at times, almost unrecognisable characters. In Josh and Benny Safdie’s Good Time (2017), Pattinson was a small-time criminal, and in Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse (2019), he played a troubled nineteenth-century lighthouse keeper stranded at a remote New England outpost.
 
Then, earlier this year, in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, Pattinson played Antinous, the main antagonist and arrogant ringleader of Queen Penelope’s suitors. Here he again faces death. In Homer’s epic, Antinous is the first suitor to be killed by an arrow to the throat, but Matt Damon, Nolan’s Odysseus, saves him for last.
 
Meanwhile, in Matt Reeves’ 2022 movie, The Batman, Bruce Wayne was not a superhuman. Pattinson portrayed Bruce Wayne as a broken “weirdo”. He was haunted by the memory of his parents’ killing in his childhood. His battle against criminals was like an unfinished attempt to heal that wound deep inside. Bruce Wayne had wealth, he relied on technology and training, and he possessed a profound sense of melancholy. In fact, Pattinson himself spoke out about the “overwhelming sadness” of The Batman.
 
Now, he faces an even greater challenge: That of being James Bond. It certainly marks a new chapter of a long-standing cultural institution. Born from the novels of Ian Fleming, James Bond first appeared on screen in 1962’s Dr. No. “Bond. James Bond” in Sean Connery’s voice has since become the signature catchphrase of the fictional MI6 agent 007 and also an iconic fixture of popular culture. Subsequently, five more actors, namely George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig, have brought their own chemistry and interpretation to the character. Each of these actors maintained the character’s foundational and distinguishable traits. But, in the process, they also left the distinct imprint of their own era.
 
The main attraction of Bond, certainly, is not just in espionage but in the dream of an extraordinary, impossible lifestyle. Sometimes he travels in an Aston Martin, sometimes in a submarine. His tuxedo remains virtually pristine even amidst explosions, the ice in his martini glass never melts, and the Bond girls keep us amazed. And his dangerous villains invariably pause to deliver quite long speeches before attempting to kill him; Bond’s survival depends much on the verbosity of his villains, too, along with his own skills!
 
Some believe that Connery is the definitive Bond. For some, it’s Moore. In fact, Sean Connery’s Bond had a dangerous, masculine charm, while Roger Moore brought a sense of humour and a lighter touch. Timothy Dalton, however, portrayed a sterner, tougher Bond, and Pierce Brosnan brought back a sense of glamour. The new generation thinks that Daniel Craig is the real Bond. Craig’s Bond, of course, is far more human.
 
Pattinson would be playing the role of the iconic spy when the very definition of a male cinematic hero has been undergoing a change. Today’s hero may not be a confident, formidable, and emotionless man as earlier. Rather, today’s audience might prefer vulnerabilities in a hero. Thus, as Pattinson intends to play Bond in a renewed worldview, he has quite a complex and formidable task ahead. He has already played diverse characters in his acting career. Now, will he be able to become both resolutely firm, loyal, and unwavering in purpose and simultaneously fragile as James Bond?
 
Cedric has died, Edward can’t die, Antinous faces a miserable death, and Batman lives with the memory of death. But Pattinson now holds a “license to kill” (and thrill!). And a “license to survive,” too!
 
 
The writer is professor of Statistics, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata
 
Eye Culture is a weekly column devoted to subjects such as art, dance, music, film, sport, and science

data.title: Funding stalemate in Indian chess: Rising players battle financial hurdles
data.description:
India has 100 chess grandmasters — up from 85 at the end of 2024 — yet players, parents and coaches say that depth masks a financial squeeze for upcoming talent: Families still fund travel and coaching while sponsors and state governments back established names.
 
Viswanathan Anand was India’s first grandmaster (GM), winning the title in 1988. 
 
Anuj Shrivatri became the country’s 100th GM on November 8 when he won the 7th Asean Plus Individual Open Chess Championship in Ozamiz City, Philippines.
 
Earning chess’ highest title from the Fédération Internationale des Échecs (FIDE) requires a 2500 rating and three “norms” across at least 27 games. Each norm is a title-qualifying performance of at least 2600 in a nine-or-more-game event against opponents averaging 2380 or higher, including at least three GMs and players from at least two other federations. 
 
An international master (IM), the step below GM, needs a 2400 rating and three norms of at least 2450 against opponents averaging 2230, including at least three IMs or GMs and players from at least two other federations.
 
“Chess is an expensive sport; you pay for travel, coaches and everything out of your own pocket if you are an individual player,” said Dr Nidhi Bhasin, who left her medical practice to travel with her daughter, a chess player. Bhasin runs Chess Coffee Connect, which assists players in accessing more opportunities.
 
“The biggest support they need is travelling to tournaments and coaching. These are the two major expenses of chess players,” said Sagar Shah, an IM and the cofounder and chief executive officer of ChessBase India. 
 
The organisation runs the nonprofit HelpChess, which raises donations to give chess players scholarships and laptops.
 
HelpChess has received “more than 400 applications” in the last year, Shah said.
 
Mohammed Imran, a 17-year-old IM from Andhra Pradesh, lacks sponsors and needs funds to compete for a GM title. He plans to complete his current title push and then quit chess to study abroad. “I have completed two out of three norms this year, I have just one norm left, but my family has paid so much for my dream,” he said.
 
Vishal Sareen, an IM and senior FIDE trainer, understands players like Imran. “I don’t think funding for players after they become a grandmaster is too much of an issue, but it is that of the transition from an IM to a GM that is an issue,” he said.
 
“There are so many players, it is very hard to give them all the monetary help. That’s why they [sponsors] just give to those already established, whereas players like Koneru Humpy get it through the oil companies that they represent,” said Sareen, referring to India’s first woman GM who plays for state-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation.  
 
Sponsorship for lesser-known players is not unheard of, though. “For example, this 10-year-old I coach was able to get ₹9 lakh in funding from different streams, of course, so yes, it isn’t that hard,” Sareen said.
 
“I think the moment you hit 2700 [norm], usually sponsors get interested,” Shah said. Oil companies are different: “This [their support] does not come in sponsorships. It comes under employment.”
 
At the top of the sport, monetary rewards are plentiful, highlighting the gap between rising aspirants and established stars. 
 
The All-India Chess Federation (AICF) gave each 2024 Olympiad gold medallist ₹25 lakh, according to ChessBase. Tamil Nadu gave Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, a GM, ₹50 lakh in June for winning the Norway Chess 2026 championship. On October 8, it gave R Praggnanandhaa and Gukesh Dommaraju, another Chennai resident and fellow GM, ₹15 lakh each for the Indian open team winning silver at this year’s Olympiad.
 
“I think we should not only award the ones at the top but also provide some monetary help to those at the bottom,” Imran said.
 
Bharat Singh Chauhan, a former AICF secretary, said the federation “tries to provide as much as we can for players. We provide them with stipends, which help them with their games. There are big companies that do sponsor the more major players of the industry.” The AICF’s stipend scheme, launched in June 2025, pays ₹60,000 to ₹1.5 lakh a quarter.
 
Bhasin, of Chess Coffee Connect, said the AICF usually restricts players from taking outside funding once it commits a set amount. Chauhan disputed that characterisation. The AICF did not respond to emails seeking comment.  
 
“One of the things that the AICF has done incredibly well is to have a very strong national system in place,” Shah said. 
 
Asked what he would change, he said: “I do feel that maybe the state and the Central governments could have a unified [player support] system in place.”
 
“It’s very difficult to cover all of them,” he said of players near the GM title. “Some do crowdfunding, some start teaching and fund themselves, some play local events to earn money, then go outside India,” Shah said. “I hope someday we could support everyone but we also have limited resources.”
 
Private backers are starting to fill part of that gap. Chola Chess, backed by Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company, hosts norm tournaments in Chennai. 
 
Aarthie Ramaswamy, a consultant for Chola Chess tournaments, said participating in a norm event may cost a contestant up to ₹15 lakh. Travelling abroad for this purpose is even more expensive.
 
“When they play tournaments in India, the cost is reduced. They can make their norms in India itself,” Ramaswamy said.
 
Even winning money can be hard to collect. GM and Arjuna awardee Abhijeet Gupta won the Odisha Open in January, but is still owed the ₹5.5 lakh prize.
 
“The organisers assured me that the prize money would be paid within a month. However, when I followed up later, they stopped responding,” he said in a news interview in May.
 
“Since the tournament was affiliated with the AICF, I also reached out to the federation’s president and secretary, hoping the matter would be resolved fairly. Unfortunately, there has been no response from them either,” he said then.
 
He wrote about the matter on X (formerly Twitter) but deleted the post later.
 
“Earlier, when you achieved a world ranking or anything, the national federation [AICF] used to give you a certain amount. This was the case if you won the title of grandmaster, international master, and many other titles. The federation no longer 
 
does that. I don’t really know why,” Gupta told Business Standard recently.
 
Tournaments in India can give rising players a way to earn. Tata Steel Chess India, held in Kolkata in January, offered $41,500 each for its men’s and women’s events. “These tournaments do significantly help in earning for the players,” said Shah of ChessBase.
 
The Global Chess League, held in Bengaluru in September, is a franchise event meant to mirror the Indian Premier League (IPL), Bhasin said, with players setting their own price tags. 
 
However, Sareen, the senior FIDE trainer, doubted it would uncover fresh talent the way the IPL does, adding: “I think it’s only for established players, because no one really knows the other players.”
 
Gupta, while speaking to Business Standard, compared India with chess leagues abroad. 
 
“I am here in the United Arab Emirates currently playing in a league. Every federation has a league. The UAE has one grandmaster and they have a league. We have [100 GMs] and still no league. It gets hard for players, and that’s when they drop out,” he said.
 
Asked about the Odisha Open prize money, he said he had signed a non-disclosure agreement with the AICF and will not comment. 
Indian GMs with sponsorship
 
Arjun Erigaisi: Sponsored by Quantbox Research at around ₹12.4 crore since 2022 over a five-year duration
 
Gukesh D: Backed by WestBridge Capital for 5 years (2024) with sponsorship estimated at ₹50 lakh to ₹1.5 crore. Apart from being RBL Bank’s brand ambassador (2024), he is also engaged in campaign work for brands such as Britannia, Amul, Cadbury, Myntra FWD and Sony TV, with an estimated ₹40 lakh-70 lakh per brand partnership
 
R Praggnanandhaa: Backed by Adani group since January 2024 under a long-term deal valued between ₹40 lakh and ₹70 lakh
 
Viswanathan Anand, Vidit Gujrathi and Nihal Sarin: While Viswanathan Anand has been a brand ambassador for tech skilling company NIIT since 1999, Vidit Gujrathi has been a brand ambassador for financial advisory Ambit since 2023; Nihal Sarin is a brand ambassador for dairy brand Akshayakalpa Organic
 
PSPB-backed Indian GMs
 
BPCL and IOCL players: BPCL has Pentala Harikrishna, Abhijeet Gupta, Vaibhav Suri, Geetha Narayanan Gopal and M. R. Venkatesh. Indian Oil has Adhiban, Ganguly, Lalith Babu, Karthikeyan Murali, Harika and Kunte
 
ONGC players: Koneru Humpy (since 2016), Vidit Gujrathi, Krishnan Sasikiran, Deep Sengupta, S P Sethuraman and Neelotpal Das
 
Note: PSPB is Petroleum Sports Promotion Board; all figures are estimates, actual not in public domain; BPCL is Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd; IOCL is Indian Oil Corp. Ltd.
Source: ChessBase India, Adani group press release, media reports

data.title: Pakistan's space capability improving with China's help: CDS Subramani
data.description:
Pakistan's space capability is "improving" with China's help, which must be "factored in into our calculus" along with their other domain-related capabilities, CDS Gen N S Raja Subramani said on Friday.

His comments, made during an interactive seminar here, came in response to a query on China successfully launching its Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship, carrying three astronauts, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, on Wednesday.

Ali is the first foreign national to participate in China's crewed space programme. His participation in China's space mission is part of the 75th anniversary of China-Pakistan diplomatic ties being celebrated by the "all-weather" allies with close defence and economic ties.

 

After delivering an address here on the 'Future of warfare and India's preparedness to conduct multi-domain operations', he fielded some questions from the audience at a session moderated by former CDS, Gen Anil Chauhan (retd), who was the Chief of Defence Staff during Operation Sindoor last year.

Asked about the participation of the Pakistani astronaut in China's space mission, Gen Raja Subramani said, "As far as your first question relating to Pakistan's space capability, yes, its space capability is improving with Chinese help. And also SUPARCO, which is a Pakistan's organisation, is working to develop its own capability." Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO) is the national space agency of Pakistan.

"Now, we also have to take it for granted that it will be helped by the Turkish too, and whatever capabilities are available with the Chinese in terms of ISR, positional navigation, timing, etc., will be available to the Pakistanis, so that we will have to factor in into our calculus. Their ISR will be better. But, for us, having factored in into our calculus, we will have to look at enhancing our capabilities," he said.

ISR refers to intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, a key factor in any warfare.

The CDS said when space-based surveillance-3 (SBS-3) programme becomes operational, it will "enhance our capabilities to a great extent".

"Simultaneously, we are also working on methods to ensure that we are able to build, as also launch more satellites. We are also working with our private sector and entrepreneurs," he added.

Gen Raja Subramani, in his address, underlined the evolving nature of technology and warfare, however, cautioning that technology superiority is "only transitory" and this will need constant improvement to stay prepared for future wars.

The general officer, elaborating on multi-domain operations, said integration of military-space architecture and the ability to communicate effectively are key to carrying out such operations.

data.title: AI-assisted piracy puts Grand Theft Auto's business model to test
data.description:
Ever since the first release in 1997, Grand Theft Auto (GTA) has been among the most popular videogames. GTA players wander around fictional landscapes, stealing cars, shooting people, and generally committing mayhem. GTA is a prime example of the products that make gaming by far the most valuable segment of the entertainment industry. 
It is estimated that global gaming (inclusive of hardware, live stream revenues, and advertising) will generate $560 billion in revenues in 2026. Just games (excluding hardware, streaming and ads) will generate $215 billion. For context, the global movie industry will earn a piddling $126 billion this year.    
A large chunk of the world’s 3.7 billion gamers play GTA. Over 512 million units of the core games have been sold, and there are countless spin-offs too. The GTA series has always been admired for its state-of-the-art quality. Every iteration of the GTA series has been cutting-edge, leveraging the best technologies of the day. Digital historians can map the evolution of the digital industry simply by the way GTA went from being 2D (two-dimensional) to 3D to HD (high-definition). 
It has been claimed (with more than a grain of truth) that GTA is the United Kingdom’s most successful export of the 21st century. It was developed by Scottish gamers at Rockstar North, originally an Edinburgh company, which is now the subsidiary of United States’ Rockstar Games. It has also always been controversial due to its violent, amoral storylines. 
Players role-play as criminals, rising through the ranks of organised crime “mobs”, with many missions and side stories. Apart from the violence and amorality, GTA has also been criticised for the demeaning ways it depicts many (not all) women characters. The game features sex-workers, “gangsters’ molls”, and realistically depicted strip clubs. The timelines range from historic, from the 1920s onwards, to fictional near-future settings. 
The locations are fictional in terms of names (Liberty City, San Fiero, Los Santos). But GTA is mostly set in US cities like New York, New Jersey, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Las Vegas, and Miami. London and Scottish locales also appear. The cities are rendered in granular detail using GPS, and 3D maps of real places. Scientists have taken GTA locales, and run simulations of flooding to see how they are affected by weather. The renders are that good (and scientists are that nerdy).    
The sixth iteration of GTA — GTA6 — released on November 19, and it has immediately led to accusations of theft and piracy. This, too, is a paradigm driven by cutting-edge technology. Rockstar has always made its money with a business model involving what many gamers consider sharp practice. First, they release a version for consoles. Then, several months later, they release a version for the personal computer (PC). Gamers who need their GTA fix end up buying it twice, or even thrice. GTA6 was released on November 19 for the Xbox Series X|S and Playstation5 (PS5/Pro) platforms, with prices ranging from €60-90 equivalent. Less than a week later, there are excellent versions available for the PC. And, these are free. 
Rockstar didn’t release them. Gamers and vibe coders using artificial intelligence (AI) pulled GTA6 from Xbox consoles and managed to get it to run on Windows PCs. A hacker group called Cyberleek had hacked into Rockstar, and leaked a large portion of the code for the Xbox version of the game. Xbox is a Microsoft product and runs on Windows. Gamers and vibe coders recompiled to make it run natively on high-end Windows PCs. 
Here’s a technical point. A console game (or any native android app for that matter) can always be run on a desktop PC by using an emulator. Emulation makes the desktop’s hardware behave like the console’s hardware (or a mobile). But it radically slows the PC down, which is a dealbreaker for a game like GTA. Instead, if the code is taken apart and recompiled, the computer needn’t throttle itself. Recompilation is essentially what the company would do to create a PC-native version. It used to take expertise, intimate coding knowledge and many man-hours. 
Vibe coders can now use AI to do this. There’s no official estimate of how many tokens were expended on which AI to do this recompilation. But the unofficial builds work smoothly and it’s been less than a week. Of course, there’s a high risk that these PC versions are also seeded with malware. And, of course, this is illegal. But surely you didn’t expect gamers who spend their days pretending to be mobsters to be restrained by moral considerations? 
The writer is a journalist

data.title: Belonging: The story of an unknown Italian who became a known Indian
data.description:
Belonging: A Journey of Love
by Sonia Gandhi
Published by Harper Collins
544 pages             ₹1,299
 
Salman Rushdie, despite his animus towards Indira Gandhi’s imposition of the Emergency in India in 1975, once wrote in The Times that the Nehru-Gandhis “made the Kennedys look like amateurs”. Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, relives the halcyon years of the family into which she married, before the happiness is brutally terminated by the assassination of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi.
 
What was comparatively absent in the public domain was her life before she settled in India. This book fills a gap in people’s knowledge and understanding of her. “My parents, Stefano and Paolina Maino; my two sisters; and I were an ordinary middle-class family known only in Orbassano, a small town in the Torino province in the northern part of Italy,” she writes. Her father was a disciplinarian who took time to reconcile himself to his second daughter’s relationship with a man from a distant country and culture.
 
 
Sonia disarmingly admits her attraction for Rajiv was love at first sight. “My heart was pounding hard, so hard I was sure it could be heard. My face was on fire, my hand trembling as I extended it forward to him. Luminous, dark eyes, in a face of striking openness, met mine for the first time. ‘How do you do?’ I replied. I knew, that very instant — it was un colpo di fulmine, a bolt of lightning.” 
 
After their marriage in February 1968, Sonia and Rajiv, then an airline pilot, led a fairly grounded existence in Delhi. “When he was at home, his friends would drop in or we’d visit them — pilot colleagues, or his school and college friends. I think with nostalgia of the days of relative freedom and ease, when we could zip around town freely on the little grey Vespa scooter Rajiv’s mother had given him, before the need for security limited our movements.” She discloses she gave birth to a baby in January 1969 who died soon after.
 
She reveals how after her brother-in-law Sanjay Gandhi received a letter of intent from the Indian government to manufacture a small car in 1970 — Maruti, now India’s biggest carmaker, with Suzuki of Japan enjoying majority control — she became associated with it. “He wanted a family member to join the board of directors of his new company. Since I was the only member who didn’t have a government job, I was asked to fill the position, which I did unquestioningly.”
 
But she and Rajiv, she says, disagreed with Sanjay and Indira on the issue of declaring the Emergency after she was unseated as a Member of Parliament by an Allahabad court judgment. She writes, “Seated at the table for a meal, we became aware of Sanjay’s stand: ‘They’ve crossed all limits. They want to finish you [Indira]. They have to be stopped.’ Rajiv suggested caution. ‘Resigning will strengthen Ma’s position in the long run,’ he said. Sanjay retorted brusquely, ‘How can you say that? They’re bent on destroying Ma and the party.’ He was in no mood to be contradicted. My mother-in-law agreed, ‘Yes, so they are.’ Watching her demeanour, Rajiv and I felt that she was allowing events to overtake her. There was no question that a concerted and relentless campaign was on, but, not being in politics, we had different views on how to respond to the challenge.” Sonia concedes there were excesses during the Emergency, but mentions that Rajiv encouraged Indira to lift it and call elections — which she did. 
 
About the anti-Sikh riots that gripped Delhi and other parts of India after Indira’s death — in mindless retaliation to two of her Sikh bodyguards being responsible — she records, “Criminal proceedings were initiated against several individuals, many of them members of the Congress Party, charged with instigating or directing some of the violence. Several cases were also registered against members of the RSS… Justice has been hard to come by for the victims.”
 
Sonia confirms she was vehemently opposed to Rajiv succeeding his mother as prime minister. “They want me to be sworn in as prime minister,” he confided in Sonia at the hospital where Indira lay dead. “You must refuse, you must say no for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you…!” she cried.
 
She doesn’t duck the difficult moments in her husband’s premiership. First, on the Muslim divorcee Shah Bano’s case — where a court ordered her former husband to pay maintenance to her, something that was overturned by her husband’s government in Parliament — she records, “I was agitated by the issue… I argued with him [Rajiv] and questioned him… The BJP predictably accused the government of indulging in ‘vote-bank politics’. And progressive liberal opinion viewed the decision as a capitulation to the conservative elements of Muslim society. 
 
However, in 2001, after seven changes of government, the Supreme Court upheld Rajiv’s stand in the 1986 ‘Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce)’ Act.”
 
Second, on the scandal that effectively prevented Rajiv’s re-election in 1989, she registers, “The year 1987 had seen the beginnings of a controversy concerning the payment of commissions in the acquisition of Bofors Howitzer guns from Sweden… He [Rajiv] was accused of being a recipient of bribes from the Bofors firm… Many years later, on February 4, 2004, with a BJP government again in power, the Delhi High Court quashed all charges against Rajiv.” However, she does not dwell on the suspicion that someone within the Congress behind Rajiv’s back might have benefitted from the deal. 
 
Having fiercely objected to Rajiv’s acceptance of the post of prime minister, she is at pains to justify her decision to enter active politics. “I had to step out and go where my duty called,” she explains, slightly unconvincingly. 
 
The crowning moment of her life was indisputably her renunciation of the honour of becoming India’s prime minister. “It’s the right decision,” her son Rahul told her when she had made up her mind.
 
Belonging is not a discovery of India in the mould of Sonia Gandhi’s grandfather-in-law. It is a readable autobiography of an unknown Italian who became a known Indian.    
 
The reviewer is a London-based journalist

data.title: Ukraine submits Black Sea truce offer, waits for Russian response: Minister
data.description:
Ukraine ??has offered ​a Black Sea ceasefire to enable ??food exports and passed this on to international allies, Kyiv's foreign ‌minister Andrii ​Sybiha said on ​Friday. 
"We are ready for ​a ceasefire. We are grateful to India, Turkey, and Egypt, which are playing ​an active and important role ‌in de-escalating tensions in the ​Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts.
